passage: The science-model deadline was tomorrow morning, and a power cut had plunged the flat into darkness. Nazia glued tiny paper leaves by torchlight, her fingers sticky. Bidisha had sent only silly stickers on the group chat all week, while the other two chatted about a cartoon. Nazia's jaw tightened. At first she wanted to keep doing everything in silence and glare at them. Instead she typed on her mother's phone: "I've done the model and both charts. Can you write the labels, and Rehan bring the poster? Please tell me by 8 tonight." Bidisha replied, "Sorry! I'll do labels now." Nazia decided that if it happened again, she would tell the teacher.

qa.q: What happened to the lights on the night before the deadline?
qa.a: There was a power cut, so Nazia worked by torchlight.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling toward her group, and how do you know?
qa.a: She was fuming and resentful: her jaw tightened after she had done the model and both charts while the others chatted.

qa.q: What could Nazia do if the others still do not help?
qa.a: Tell the teacher calmly what she has done and what is still undone.

qa.q: How might Bidisha see Nazia's message?
qa.a: She replied "Sorry! I'll do labels now," so she likely saw it as a clear, fair request and realised she had been slack.

grounding: A child who did most of the project while others chatted feels resentful, clearly asks for tasks to be split, and plans to tell the teacher if it continues.

passage:
"Tejas, your Chandrika Atya once did a whole group project alone. I was eleven. We had to make a model of the water cycle. Four of us. But the other three just chatted and giggled, every day.
I did everything. Cutting, gluing, painting. And I said nothing. I just got angrier and angrier.
The night before, I was up till midnight, crying over the glue.
My mother said, 'Why didn't you tell them to do their part?' I hadn't thought I could.
Next project, I said on day one: 'Let's split the jobs.' When one girl still didn't help, I told the teacher. It was so much easier."

qa.q: What model did young Chandrika's group have to make?
qa.a: A model of the water cycle.

qa.q: How did young Chandrika feel doing everything alone?
qa.a: She felt angry and resentful, getting angrier every day and ending up crying over the glue.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed how young Chandrika handled group work?
qa.a: Her mother asking why she didn't tell them to do their part, after which she split jobs on day one and told the teacher when needed.

qa.q: How might the other three group members have seen the project?
qa.a: They may not have realised how much work Chandrika was doing, since she said nothing.

grounding: An aunt recalls silently doing most of a group project while others chatted; later she asked clearly for tasks to be split and told the teacher.

passage:
The history poster was due Friday, and it had rained so hard all week that the school library was closed. Ayesha had done most of the research on her mother's phone at home, and all the drawing.
Sachin and the others spent every group period chatting about cricket.
On Thursday, Ayesha's hands were shaking with anger. She wanted to throw the markers at them.
Instead she said, "I've done the research and the drawing. Sachin, can you write the captions? Priya, the border? We need to finish today."
Sachin looked surprised. "Oh. Okay."
The others picked up pens. Ayesha felt relieved. If they hadn't helped, she'd decided she would tell Mrs Joshi.

qa.q: Why was the school library closed?
qa.a: It had rained so hard all week.

qa.q: How did Ayesha feel on Thursday?
qa.a: She felt angry and resentful, her hands shaking, wanting to throw the markers.

qa.q: What did Ayesha do that was better than doing everything silently?
qa.a: She clearly asked each group mate to take a task, with a plan to tell the teacher if they didn't.

qa.q: How might Sachin feel when Ayesha gives him a job?
qa.a: Sachin seemed surprised, maybe not having realised how much Ayesha was doing.

grounding: A girl does most of a project while others chat and is fuming; she asks clearly for tasks to be split, ready to tell the teacher if it continues.
